title: 'Huge black hole' in soil knowledge despite £65m SFI spend
excerpt: DEFRA spent more than £65m on SFI soil assessment actions without routinely collecting the results produced by farmers.
content:
Soil health

1st October 2026

Author: Alfie White

DEFRA spent more than £65m on SFI soil assessment actions without routinely collecting the results produced by farmers, an FOI request has revealed.

Between 2023 and 2026, a total of 74,617 farm businesses participated in the SAM1 and CSAM1 soil actions, receiving £65.38 million across almost 10.9 million hectares.

Farmers participating in the actions were paid to assess the health of their soils, produce a soil management plan and test soil organic matter.

However, a Freedom of Information request by the Sustainable Soils Alliance (SSA) found that the results of these tests were not routinely collected.

Government guidance for CSAM1 stated that soil data was one of the “public goods” the action was paying for and said DEFRA, or the RPA, could ask farmers to provide assessment and organic matter results to improve national soil data.

“Missed opportunity”

Matthew Orman, co-executive director of the Sustainable Soils Alliance, said there was a “huge black hole” in understanding the state of the English soils, as well as farmers’ knowledge of them and the support needed to make changes.

He said the information could have provided a better understanding of both the condition of agricultural soils and how farmers use soil data.

Mr Orman told Farmers Guide: “I think they could have collected data, not just the raw data in terms of the actual numbers that farmers get from their soil assessments or their carbon numbers.

“They could have also collected insights about how farmers feel about soil data, how they feel about the value of data, full stop, in informing farm-led decisions.”

Future soil funding

Mr Orman urged DEFRA to look at the approach taken in Northern Ireland, where participation in the Soil Nutrient Health Scheme (SNHS) is a condition for receiving the Farm Sustainability Payment.

The scheme aims to sample every field in Northern Ireland and provide farmers with a baseline soil nutrient status for their farm.

He said: “We urge DEFRA to learn from the experience of Northern Ireland, which has demonstrated how a funded baseline programme, tied to conditionality, can generate usable data and drive practice change.”

DEFRA currently monitors the environmental outcomes of its ELM schemes through several methods, including ecological field surveys on a sample of participating farms and data collected through the Natural Capital and Ecosystem Assessment (NCEA).

Mr Orman added that combining farmer-generated soil information with NCEA data could be difficult because measurements needed to be taken consistently.

Factors including sampling depth, time of year, methodology and the metrics being recorded can all affect results.

He said the two forms of information nevertheless had different and potentially complementary purposes.

He said: “NCEA is about the state of the country’s soils, which feeds into the Environmental Improvement Plan target, whereas the farmer-led data ought to support on-farm decision-making.”

“But that doesn’t mean the two can’t coexist. They are different parts of the same picture.”

“Maintaining healthy soil vital”

The SSA is calling for a more consistent approach to on-farm and national soil measurement, alongside a central data hub where information could be held.

When contacted by Farmers Guide about the SAM1 and CSAM1 soil actions and whether they represented a missed opportunity for the government, a DEFRA spokesperson said: “Maintaining healthy soil is vital for Britain’s food security.

“Sustainable Farming Incentive-funded Soil Management Plans empower farmers to understand the condition of their soil, monitor changes over time and make informed management decisions to improve soil health on their land.

“We monitor the outcomes of Environmental Land Management schemes in a number of ways, including sending surveyors to visit sample farms and using data captured through the Natural Capital and Ecosystem Assessment, which is designed to monitor and map England’s natural assets.”
